title: Micah
subtitle: the prophet from the foothills who saw ruin and a mountain
lead: Micah of Moresheth was a countryman from the low hills southwest of Jerusalem who spoke in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, the years when Assyria swallowed the northern kingdom and marched into Judah. His book is seven chapters of poetry in three rounds. Each begins with the same call, "Hear" (1:2; 3:1; 6:1), and each moves from judgment to hope. The judgment is aimed at the capitals: Samaria's idols and wealth, and Jerusalem's rulers who take bribes, seize family land and say that no harm can come to a city with the LORD's house in it.

The hope is just as sharp. The same mountain that will be plowed like a field (3:12) will be the highest mountain on earth, where the nations come to be taught and swords become plowshares (4:1-5). A ruler will come from Bethlehem (5:2). The LORD will pardon the guilt of the remnant of his people and cast their sins into the depths of the sea (7:18-19). Micah is the book where the Old Testament asks most plainly what the LORD requires, and the book ends with the question that is Micah's own name: "Who is a God like you?"
facts: Micah of Moresheth, named in 1:1 and by the elders in Jeremiah 26:18. The book is in the third person at times and probably went through editing. How much of it is Micah's own is debated.

The heading puts Micah in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (about 750 to 686 BC). Samaria fell in 722/721 BC (foretold in 1:6) and Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC (1:10-16). Some critics date chapters 4-5 and 7:8-20 to the exile or after.
The kingdom of Judah in the Assyrian age; Moresheth-gath in the Shephelah, and Jerusalem
Prophetic poetry in speeches: judgment oracles, a lament, promises, a lawsuit (6:1-8) and a closing psalm-like prayer and praise (7:14-20)
Hebrew. Chapter 1:10-16 is among the hardest Hebrew in the prophets.

Chapters 1 to 3 and 6 to 7 are numbered alike in the English and Hebrew Bibles. Hebrew chapter 4 has 14 verses: its first 13 equal English 4:1-13, and its 14th is English 5:1. English 5:2-15 are Hebrew 5:1-14, so Hebrew chapter 5 has 14 verses. The Plain, the notes and the cross-references all use the English numbers.
The sixth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum...); the third in the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum...).
Found in the Dead Sea Scrolls

Hebrew manuscripts of the Twelve with Micah include 4QXIIg (4Q82), 4QXIIf (4Q81, cited in the notes on chapter 5) and Murabba'at 88 (Mur88), all close to the Masoretic Text where they can be read. The Qumran commentaries 1QpMic and 4QpMic are fragmentary and are not quoted here. The Greek Minor Prophets scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) was not collated for chapters 1 to 4, so this list is not a full survey of the scrolls.
authorship: Micah the Morashtite wrote the whole book in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Jewish tradition says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote down the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a).

Most critics think Micah's own words are mainly in chapters 1 to 3 and perhaps parts of 6; that chapters 4 and 5, and 7:8-20, grew up in later centuries, in the exile and after; and that the book was shaped in stages into its three-round form. Wolff and Mays are examples of this broad position.

Waltke and others argue that the book is a unit from the 8th century, that the hope passages answer the threats and the style is the same, and that the same sentence of 3:12 is not undone by the later hope.

audience.to: The people of Judah, above all the rulers and landowners of Jerusalem and the Shephelah, in the later 700s BC; and the readers of the book after them, in the exile and the Persian period, who read it as the word of the LORD for a people who had lost the land.
audience.why: To tell Judah what Samaria's fall means for them, to charge the rulers and prophets with the crimes that were wrecking the people (land seizure, corrupt courts, paid prophecy), and to give a reason to hope. A farmer from a country town, Micah speaks for those who lost their land; later readers heard in him a promise that the LORD would gather the lame and pardon the remnant. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the same book is a warning to the powerful, a lament for the dispossessed and a promise to the exiles.
views: The people of Judah in Hezekiah's day
The speeches were first for Judah during the Assyrian crisis (for example Mays and Waltke). Jeremiah 26:18-19 says Micah's sentence on Zion was heard and heeded.
The book as it stands was shaped for those who had lived through 586 BC and needed both the explanation (the rulers' guilt) and the promise (4:1-8; 7:8-20) (for example Wolff and Hillers).
As part of the Book of the Twelve, Micah is read beside Hosea, Amos, Jonah and Nahum as the voice of the 8th century in a collection that looks ahead to the day of the LORD (Nogalski, Sweeney).

The prophet's lament and the towns of the Shephelah
Woe to those who take fields and houses
The dispute with those who say "Do not rant"
The gathering of the remnant and the breaker
Prophets for pay, and Micah's claim of the Spirit

False measures and the statutes of Omri
Confession and hope: the enemy falls
Prayer for the flock and praise of the God who pardons

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads Micah in the 700s BC: Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah; the Syro-Ephraimite crisis; the fall of Samaria in 722/721 BC; Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC and the Shephelah towns (Lachish, Mareshah, Moresheth-gath); the Lachish reliefs and Sennacherib's own annals; and what the later history of Zion did and did not fulfill (586 BC, the return, AD 70).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made and when. The debates: the three-round structure, whether chapters 4-5 and 7:8-20 are post-exilic additions (Mays, Wolff, Hillers, Andersen-Freedman, Allen, Waltke, Smith), the very hard Hebrew of 1:10-16, the relation of 4:1-5 to Isaiah 2:2-4, and the Greek, Dead Sea and Targum witnesses.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Micah as Jews have: Jeremiah 26's quotation of 3:12, the Talmud's story of Rabbi Akiva laughing at the ruin of the Temple (Makkot 24b), Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak, the Targum, the haftarot (5:6-6:8; 7:18-20) and Micah 6:8 in the Talmud's reduction of the 613 commandments.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Micah as the church has: the fathers (Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Jerome, Theodoret, Cyril), the quotation of 5:2 in Matthew 2:5-6 and of 7:6 in Matthew 10:35-36, the peace of 4:1-4, Calvin and Luther, and the debate over works and grace around 6:8.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads the promises as future: the nations at Zion (4:1-8), the ruler from Bethlehem (5:2-5) and the pardon of 7:18-20, with the views of those who see them as fulfilled in Christ and the church, those who look for a restored Israel and Jerusalem, and those who take them as hope without a timetable.

sections.b: Micah is poetry and mostly short speeches, so read it a speech at a time. The book is built in three rounds that each begin "Hear": 1:2 (all the peoples), 3:1 (the rulers of Jacob), 6:1 (the mountains, as a jury in the LORD's lawsuit). Each round goes from judgment to hope: 2:12-13, then 4:1-5:15, then 7:8-20. The Plain marks poetic lines with " / ". Three words recur and are kept distinct: mishpat ("justice", the rulers' task), pesha' ("rebellion"), and she'erit ("remnant", what is left). The book also plays on sound: place names in chapter 1 (the glosses give the English), the verb "plan" in 2:1 and 2:3, "wind" and "Spirit" (ruach) in 2:7, 2:11 and 3:8, and Micah's own name, "Who is like the LORD?", in 7:18.

sections.h: The three rounds in a sentence each
sections.b: Round one (1:2-2:13). The LORD comes down against Samaria, Micah mourns the towns of the Shephelah, the land-grabbers are condemned, and the LORD promises to gather the remnant. Round two (3:1-5:15). The rulers and prophets are condemned, Zion will be plowed (3:12), and then Zion is the world's mountain (4:1-5); the lame become a remnant; a ruler comes from Bethlehem (5:2); the LORD cleanses the land. Round three (6:1-7:20). The LORD's lawsuit and what he requires (6:8), the false measures, the prophet's lament, and the closing praise of the God who pardons.

Micah speaks at the same time as Isaiah in Jerusalem and Hosea and Amos in the north. The oracle of 4:1-3 is also in Isaiah 2:2-4, and Jeremiah 26:18 is the clearest case in the Bible of one prophet's words being quoted by name and date. Micah's charges (land, courts, paid prophets) are close to Isaiah 5 and Amos 2. His answer to the question of what the LORD requires (6:8) has been called the summary of the prophets.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians have used Micah
sections.b: In synagogue worship Micah appears in the haftarot, among them Micah 5:6-6:8 (with Parashat Balak) and Micah 7:18-20 on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Christians have read Micah 5:2 as pointing to the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:5-6), 4:3 as the peace of Christ's kingdom, and 7:6 in Jesus' words about households divided (Matthew 10:35-36). Both traditions treat 3:12 as a standing warning to the powerful.

The Hebrew text is mostly sound, with some very hard passages: 1:10-16, 2:6-11, 6:9-16 and parts of 7. The Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus) differs in those places. The Dead Sea scrolls 4Q82 (4QXIIg) and Mur88 agree with the Masoretic Text where they are readable; where they are damaged, the variants say so. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text of the Leningrad Codex everywhere in chapters 1 to 4, and the variants list each case where the Greek reads otherwise.

spec.title: The book as a trial that ends in pardon
spec.body: The book's three "Hear" speeches (1:2; 3:1; 6:1) look like the stages of a trial. The first summons the witnesses (the peoples) and states the charge (Jacob's rebellion). The second addresses the officials who were meant to judge and shows them the sentence. The third is the formal lawsuit (6:1-8). The ending reverses it: the same LORD who testified against his people now pardons guilt and throws all their sins into the depths of the sea (7:18-19). My theory is that the whole book is built to turn a courtroom into a place of pardon, with the question "Who is like the LORD?" in the heading's name and in the last verses as the hinge. This overlaps with scholars who treat the lawsuit form and the name-pun at 7:18 as frames (Mays, Waltke), but the claim that the entire book follows a trial sequence from witnesses to verdict to pardon is my own reading.

prompts: A hand-drawn scroll illustration in ink and ochre of a tall figure of light stepping down from a temple among clouds onto a range of mountains that melt like candle wax into the valleys, with tiny houses and fields below. Soft torn edges like old parchment, cave-drawing style animals along the margin, a few Hebrew letters, no hard rectangle.

A sketch on aged papyrus in the style of an ancient map: low hills with small walled towns, each with a tiny symbol (dust, a horse, a bride's veil, a dry streambed), and a farmer in the foreground tearing his clothes and walking barefoot. Soft uneven borders, charcoal and earth colors.

A hand-drawn picture, half cave painting and half modern line art: people from many nations climbing a mountain, hammering swords into plows and spears into pruning hooks beside a vine and fig tree where a family sits at peace. Soft edges, parchment texture, no hard border.
reading: Bruce K. Waltke, A Commentary on Micah (Eerdmans, 2007)
A full commentary that defends the book's unity and gives the history of Jewish and Christian interpretation.
James Luther Mays, Micah, Old Testament Library (1976)
Hans Walter Wolff, Micah: A Commentary (Augsburg, 1990)
A detailed critical commentary that traces how the book grew.
A careful commentary on the Hebrew text and its difficulties.
Leslie C. Allen, The Books of Joel, Obadiah, Jonah and Micah, NICOT (1976)
A balanced commentary for readers who want the Hebrew explained.
David Ussishkin, The Conquest of Lachish by Sennacherib (1982)
The excavation and the Assyrian relief that illustrate 1:13.
